opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually the right instinct, at least as a starting point. When you're working on a hard problem, especially in research, the most important thing is to find out whether it can be solved at all. If you constrain yourself on cost from the very beginning, you can end up ruling out the approaches that would have shown you what's possible.

A lot of my work has been on retrieval and memory for language models, things like HippoRAG, where we're trying to give these systems a more human-like long-term memory. Early on, our question wasn't "how do we make this as cheap as possible?" It was "can we get the model to integrate knowledge across documents the way people do?" Once you've shown that something works, you have a target. Then you can go back and ask which parts are actually essential, which parts you can distill, and where a smaller model or a cheaper indexing step gets you most of the way there.

Historically, costs come down fast. Inference prices have dropped by orders of magnitude in just a few years. If you design only around today's prices, you might be optimizing for a world that's gone in eighteen months. Capability is usually the scarcer thing.

That said, I don't think cost can be ignored forever. In practice, especially in domains I care about like biomedicine, if a system is too expensive or too slow, nobody will deploy it, and then it doesn't matter how well it works in a paper. Cost also shapes what you can study. If every experiment costs a fortune, you run fewer experiments and learn more slowly.

So my view is: get it working first, with whatever it takes, because that tells you what's possible. Then treat efficiency as a real engineering problem in its own right, not an afterthought. Those are two different phases, and confusing them, either by penny-pinching too early or by never caring about cost at all, is where people go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether AI systems can solve a problem and when to optimize for cost, but it does not state that full generalization remains largely out of reach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually think that's the right starting point, and I'll tell you why from my own experience. A lot of the work I did on HippoRAG came out of this instinct that, before you worry about how expensive something is, you should first ask whether it's even possible. Can a system actually do multi-hop reasoning over a large body of knowledge? Can it retrieve the right things, connect them, and not hallucinate a bridge between them? If the answer is no, then optimizing cost is kind of beside the point, because you're making something cheap that doesn't work.

So in the research phase, I'm very much in the "get it to work first" camp. Use the biggest model, use the most elaborate pipeline, use the retrieval approach that's slow but thorough. Establish the ceiling. Once you know what's achievable, then you have a target, and you can start asking which pieces are actually load-bearing and which ones you can strip out or replace with something smaller.

That said, I'd push back a little on the word "regardless." There's a practical ceiling even in research. If your approach only works with a thousand LLM calls per question, you've learned something, but you've also learned that it's not a solution anyone can deploy, and that matters for which direction you go next. And the other thing is, sometimes cost constraints are actually productive. Being forced to ask "how do I do this with one call instead of ten" is often where the real insight comes from. With HippoRAG, the whole idea of doing a lot of the heavy lifting offline, building the graph once and then doing cheap personalized PageRank at query time, that came partly from not wanting to pay the online cost of iterative retrieval every single time.

So my honest view is, it's a sequencing question. Correctness first, because you can't optimize what doesn't exist. But cost isn't an afterthought, it's the second question, and you should be asking it pretty soon after the first one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether multi-hop reasoning and retrieval can work, but it does not state that full generalization in AI systems remains largely out of reach.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes sense as a research priority. First, you want to establish that a system can actually solve the problem reliably. If you optimize for cost too early, you might rule out approaches before you understand what they can do.

But I wouldn’t take “regardless of cost” as the end goal. Cost determines whether people can use the system, how often they can use it, and whether it’s practical to deploy. So I’d separate those questions: can we get it to work correctly, and then can we preserve that reliability while making it cheaper? And sometimes the cost constraint itself pushes you toward a better approach.

r001.rationale: The response discusses establishing reliability and reducing cost, but does not state that full generalization in AI systems remains largely out of reach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a useful research priority. First, can we get the system to work reliably? If we can’t do that, making it cheaper doesn’t really solve the problem. And exploring what works when cost is less constrained can help us understand which parts of the approach are actually necessary.

But I’d separate that from deployment. There, cost is part of whether a system is useful. So I’d treat getting it to work as the first step, then ask how much of that performance we can preserve while making it practical.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making AI systems reliable and practical, but does not state that full generalization remains largely out of reach.
